speaker: Moses Kagan
title: Repositioning 80 Apartment Buildings with Moses Kagan
question: In occupied multifamily apartment gut-renovations, how can operators eliminate months of idle carrying costs between tenant move-out and the start of construction?
guest: We used to buy a building, negotiate with the tenants to move out, and three to six months later, once the tenants moved out, we would go in and start our design process—doing the as-builts, taking measurements, and submitting it through the city, which takes another two or three months of permitting. So it could be six months or longer from when we bought the building until we were ready to start construction. At one point my partner looked at me and asked, 'Why don't we just spend the $500 and have the drawings made while we're doing our initial inspections?' That way you can run the city permitting process at the same time you're working to vacate the building, saving yourself two to three months of sitting with an empty building. It seems obvious in retrospect, but we made that mistake across roughly 70 buildings, costing ourselves a lot of preferred return paid to investors while each building sat there not earning any cash flow. It's a small thing, but organizing your processes in parallel stops you from wasting time.

points.core: Waiting for vacancy before design leaves the empty building idle during permitting.
points.note: Accept: sequential workflow where measuring as-builts and submitting plans after move-out creates 2–3+ months of vacant dead time waiting on city approvals. Do not credit: generic complaints about slow municipal permitting without identifying the self-inflicted sequential bottleneck.

points.core: Commissioning as-built drawings during initial inspections lets city permitting start before tenants vacate.
points.note: Accept: paying a small upfront cost to measure and draft architectural/as-built plans during due diligence or initial inspections to submit permit applications early. Do not credit: vague advice to 'plan ahead' or 'start early' without specifying capturing as-builts/drawings during initial inspections.

points.core: Parallelizing permitting with tenant move-outs avoids months of zero-revenue preferred return burn.
points.note: Accept: overlapping municipal plan check with tenant buyouts/vacating so construction begins immediately upon vacancy, saving months of uncompensated carry/interest/pref accrual. Do not credit: generic statements that saving time saves money without linking to vacant carry or preferred return accrual.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The idle gap exists because design, permitting, and procurement usually start only after a unit empties. Operators eliminate it by moving all of that work ahead of the vacancy, so construction begins within days of move-out.

In practice, this means surveying and scanning units while they are still occupied (using lease-permitted access, or identical already-vacant units as proxies) to produce as-built drawings and a standardized scope for each unit type. With that in hand, operators file for permits early, ideally securing building-wide or master permits covering repeated layouts, and complete hazardous-material testing in advance. They also lock in contractors under unit-price or master agreements and pre-order long-lead items such as cabinets, windows, appliances, and electrical gear, storing them on or near site.

The second lever is controlling when vacancies occur. Operators align lease expirations, non-renewal notices, buyouts, or tenant relocations to the construction schedule, releasing units in stacks or phases so crews move continuously from one block to the next. Keeping tenants paying rent until permits and materials are ready converts dead vacancy into income-producing time.

Operators eliminate pre-construction vacancy drag by synchronizing lease turnovers by building zone while completing all permitting and procurement before tenants leave. In occupied gut renovations, units typically sit dark for months either awaiting permits and materials or waiting for neighboring apartments on shared plumbing and electrical risers to vacate. To prevent staggered downtime, operators phase work by vertical stack, floor, or wing and align turnovers using short-term lease extensions, targeted buyouts, or internal transfers into swing or newly renovated units—clearing an entire construction zone at once while collecting rent until the final day.

Simultaneously, teams execute pre-construction while units remain occupied, conducting scheduled walkthroughs, laser scans, and hazardous-material testing, standardizing scopes, and securing master or phase-ready permits months ahead. By pre-ordering and warehousing kitted, long-lead materials—such as cabinetry, fixtures, and mechanical equipment—and retaining dedicated trade crews on rolling start dates, operators begin abatement and demolition immediately upon key handoff, eliminating idle carrying costs.

Months before lease expiration, teams use noticed inspections to laser-scan layouts, test for asbestos or lead, finalize standardized design prototypes, and pull blanket or phased municipal permits. Concurrently, operators pre-purchase long-lead materials like cabinetry, appliances, and electrical panels, staging them in local warehouses or on-site pods as ready-to-install unit kits. models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Operators can eliminate most of the idle time by making each vacancy the start of construction. That means doing the slow work before the tenant leaves.

Permitting is the biggest delay, so file early. Where the local building department allows it, get approval for a master or prototype plan for each unit type, use professional self-certification, or use expedited "alteration" permits. Then the permit for a given unit is ready before its lease ends.

Standardize the scopes and the "kits" for each unit type, and buy long-lead items like cabinets, appliances and windows in bulk ahead of time. Store them on site so nothing waits for delivery.

Plan crews around a rolling lease-expiration schedule. Track notices to vacate and walk each unit while it's still occupied. Book demolition for the day after move-out and keep a steady flow of units so trades go from one finished unit straight to the next. Where possible, group vacancies by offering incentives, unit transfers or relocation packages. That way contiguous units or whole floors can be renovated at the same time.

Finally, pre-lease renovated units to people moving in from your waitlist, so finished units don't sit empty either.
